one_liner: Rust std HashMap counting 4-grams, 1.54x faster than the best C/C++ build (std::unordered_map) in LangArena Distance::NGram.
what_it_does: A LangArena benchmark row, not a library: about 70 lines of Rust (rust/src/benchmarks/distance.rs, NGram::ngram) that score the 4-gram overlap of 10 random string pairs over a 10-letter alphabet. Each 4-gram is packed into a u32 and counted in std::collections::HashMap<u32, i32> pre-sized with with_capacity(len); the second string is counted while probing the first map, and the score is intersection / (distinct grams 1 + distinct grams 2). What you copy is the pattern (pack n-grams into integers, count in a pre-sized flat map), not an API.
how_it_is_fast: Rust's std HashMap is hashbrown, a port of Google's SwissTable (open addressing with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup of control bytes), so keys and counts sit inline in the reserved table and an insert does not allocate. libstdc++ std::unordered_map is node-based: each of the 122,691 distinct-key inserts per run (from my replay of the workload) allocates a node that is freed again when the map dies inside the timed loop, about 12.3 million malloc/free pairs over 100 timed runs, and every probe walks bucket-to-node pointers. Rust wins although it hashes with SipHash-1-3, which its own docs say other hashers beat for integer keys, while libstdc++ hashes integers with the identity function. The win comes from the container layout, not from code generation.
when_to_use: Counting small integer keys (packed n-grams, k-mers, IDs) in a map that is built, probed and dropped per call, where a node-based map spends its time in malloc and free.
Picking a language for text-similarity or k-mer counting code that must stick to standard containers: Rust's default HashMap is already a flat SwissTable, while C++'s std::unordered_map is not.
Maps of up to about 10^4 keys pre-sized with with_capacity, as measured (at most 8,647 keys per map, 10,000 possible 4-grams).
Evidence that std::unordered_map, not the compiler, is the bottleneck in a C++ counting loop before you swap containers.
when_not_to_use: If you are staying in C++: replacing std::unordered_map with absl::flat_hash_map, boost::unordered_flat_map or ankerl::unordered_dense (all in this catalogue's hash-maps-sets category) probably closes the gap without a rewrite. This is inference; the suite only allows standard containers (the maintainer closed PR #11, an HPPC primitive-map patch for the Java NGram test, on that ground).

Hash-bound workloads on trusted input: the default SipHash-1-3 is slow for u32 keys. A faster hasher via with_capacity_and_hasher (FxHash, foldhash) would probably go further than the measured row, but that is not measured.
Key sets far larger than cache: the test never holds more than 8,647 keys per map, so there is no evidence for millions of keys.

As a Rust-beats-C++ codegen claim: Zig 0.52 s, C# 0.516 s, Julia 0.58 s, Go 0.603 s and even Rust compiled to WebAssembly under Node (0.473 s) beat every C/C++ row, and the C rows (uthash, a malloc per distinct gram, 1.79-1.84 s) are slower still.
Decisions that hinge on a few percent: one measurement per configuration, and the C++/G++ prod row drifted between 0.839 and 0.908 s across six monthly runs with unchanged code.

integration.dependencies: none (Rust std::collections::HashMap); the benchmark crate's serde_json, regex and similar dependencies serve other tests and the harness
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2021 (rust/Cargo.toml); measured with rustc 1.99.0 and the default release profile (opt-level 3, 16 codegen units, no LTO, no target-cpu)
integration.platforms: Measured only on x86-64 Linux (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X); the code is portable safe Rust with nothing platform-specific
integration.thread_safety: Not shared: each call builds two local maps; HashMap has no internal locking and mutation needs an exclusive &mut borrow. The benchmark is single-threaded.

gotchas: Harness check, no flaw found. My Python replay of the run.js workload (fasta LCG, period 139,968) gives 10 pairs with 213,051 characters, at most 8,647 keys per map, 122,691 distinct-key inserts and 320,106 hash operations per run, and reproduces the expected checksum 397440 as 120 runs (20 untimed warm-up plus 100 timed) of 3,312. benchmarks.rb records a runtime only when the binary prints '<test>: OK in Xs', runs each test in its own process and takes peak RSS from /usr/bin/time; both harnesses time only run_all with a monotonic clock, and both include map destruction.

The Rust test was tuned on 2026-09-06 (commit 9ebdaec, 'reuse the NGram map entry', AI co-authored like much of the suite). Before it, Rust looked the s2 gram up a second time and led the best C/C++ row by 1.32-1.40x (2026-06-16 to 2026-09-03 results); afterwards the lead is 1.51-1.54x. The change matches the C++ try_emplace logic, so the current figure is the like-for-like one. cpp/src/distance.cpp is unchanged since 2026-04-24.

The headline Rust row is not Rust's best: the default release profile uses 16 codegen units, and Rust/WMO (codegen-units 1, 0.388 s) and Rust/PGO (0.387 s) are about 2.1x faster than the best C/C++ row. Rust also builds without -march=native, while the C++ Fast, Unsafe and PGO rows lose despite -O3 -march=native or profile data.

The C/C++ toolchain is GCC 16.0.1 '(experimental)' trunk r16-8246 and Clang 22.1.8. The -flto flags in cpp/Makefile appear only on the link line (objects compile without -flto), so the 'LTO' variants get no LTO; that matters little here because the hot code is in one file.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against the Zig (0.52 s, 3.4 MB) and Go (0.603 s, 12.0 MB) rows of the same test, Rust prod is in the same band (0.533 s, 4.3 MB) but has the best tuned builds (0.388 s with codegen-units 1, 0.387 s with PGO), so pick it when you want a memory-safe default map with low RSS and headroom from build settings. If you must stay in C++, the hash-maps-sets entries (abseil, Boost.Unordered, unordered_dense) are the direct fix.
verified_claims_summary: In the 2026-10-05 LangArena run on an AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, the Rust test (rustc 1.99.0, default release profile, std HashMap with SipHash) took 0.533 s for 100 timed iterations. The best of 16 C/C++ builds, C++/Clang++ 22.1.8 PGO with libstdc++ std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int>, took 0.822 s, and the -O2 prod builds took 0.863 s (G++ 16.0.1) and 0.877 s (Clang++), so Rust is 1.54x and 1.62x faster (derived from the results file). Peak RSS was 4.3 MB against 6.6-7.1 MB.
status_note: LangArena is MIT-licensed and actively maintained, re-run about monthly (last commit 2026-10-08, 41 stars); this is a benchmark row rather than a library, so copy the pattern (u32-packed n-grams in a pre-sized flat map), and in C++ get the same effect by switching to a flat hash map.
